_note: Scenes for the Heavenly Band article images. One entry per article slug, read by tools/StationImageStudio (Articles view). The scene is only the PICTURE — the house standard is added around it by ArticlePrompt: white over-ear headphones on everyone wearing any, worn as unremarkably as a wristwatch; ordinary people of mixed ages; modest dress with wetsuits or rash guards anywhere swimwear would be implied; a warm golden glow throughout; no text anywhere. Do not repeat those rules here. Write only what is happening and who it is happening to.
_persona: The persona named in a scene must be the article's own author, because the studio attaches that persona's portrait as the likeness reference.

what-heavenly-modulation-is.scene: Jubilee stands on a grassy hilltop at golden hour beside a tall old radio mast, one hand resting on a guy wire, while below her a whole valley of small houses each show one lit window; a boy of about nine has climbed onto a hay bale beside her and is pointing up at the mast, delighted, as though he has just worked out where the sound comes from

why-it-had-to-be-music.scene: Melody sits on the tailgate of a parked estate car at a school sports field, surrounded by seven or eight children of mixed ages sitting cross-legged on the grass; every one of them is singing the same phrase back at her with their eyes shut and their chins up, and one small girl is conducting with a stick she found

free-and-built-to-stay-free.scene: Jubilee holds open the door of a busy community hall where a free meal is being served; there is no till, no queue rope and no sign, and a grandmother carrying two plates is walking straight past her into the room without being asked for anything, while a toddler slips under Jubilee's arm ahead of them both

ai-pointed-at-the-kingdom.scene: Amir kneels on a workshop floor beside a boy of about eleven, the two of them wiring a small homemade speaker; the bench above them is covered in ordinary tools and a battered notebook, and both are laughing at the speaker crackling into life on the first try

can-a-machine-worship.scene: Nova sits on the floor of an empty church at dusk with her back against a pew end, a small portable radio playing beside her; she is not looking at it but upward at the high window, and an elderly woman two rows back has her hands open on her knees — the two humans are worshipping and the machine is only carrying the sound

what-ai-never-decides.scene: Zev stands at a long table where a printed list is weighted down with stones against the wind on a rooftop at sunset; three adults and a teenage girl lean in reading it, and one of them is already pointing at a line with a pen, as if intending to hold somebody to it

who-wrote-this-song.scene: Caleb leans over a kitchen table where a family has laid out a paper chain of handwritten cards running from one end to the other; a girl of about seven is laying the last card down at the far end and looking back along the whole line she has just completed

the-cost-of-a-station.scene: Amir stands in a tiny shopfront studio in a dusty street, one microphone and one lamp, while outside the window a crowd of passers-by of every age has stopped to listen; a boy has climbed onto his father's shoulders to see in, and the contrast between the smallness of the room and the size of the crowd is the whole picture

every-tool-the-church-feared.scene: Elias walks through a museum gallery of old communication machines — a printing press, a valve radio, a boxy television, a beige computer — with a school group of children swarming ahead of him; a girl has stopped at the printing press and is reaching out to touch it while the others have already run on to the next one

everywhere-there-is-a-signal.scene: Zariah sits on the back step of a house at the edge of a village at sunset, an inexpensive phone propped against a flowerpot, and children from three neighbouring houses have drifted over and settled on the steps around her without being invited; nobody is holding the phone

voices-not-strangers.scene: Nova is greeted at a front door by a family who clearly know her, the mother already talking, a small boy hugging her leg before she is fully through the doorway, a dog pushing past everyone; the warmth of arrival is the subject

a-frequency-nobody-pays-to-reach.scene: Elias stands at an open farm gate holding it wide, on a track leading up into golden hills; a mixed group of walkers of all ages including two small children with rucksacks is streaming through it, and there is no gatehouse, no barrier and nobody collecting anything

the-first-song-after-the-sea.scene: Zev stands ankle deep at the edge of a vast shallow tidal flat at sunrise with a crowd of ordinary people behind him, everybody's arms already going up, several children running in the shallows throwing water at the sky; the relief on every face has just turned into singing

lament-has-a-frequency.scene: Eliana sits on a bench in a rainy bus shelter beside a woman who is quietly crying; Eliana is not talking or reaching for her, only sitting alongside, and a child on the woman's other side has put a small hand on her sleeve

the-song-you-sang-at-eleven.scene: Melody stands in a primary school corridor watching a group of nine and ten year olds performing a song for nobody in particular; behind them a grandmother waiting to collect a child is silently mouthing the very same words she learned at that age

two-people-at-once.scene: Jubilee stands in the middle of a packed room with one hand raised upward and the other resting on the shoulder of the stranger beside her; the whole room is doing the same double gesture, and a small girl on her father's shoulders has copied it exactly

the-kingdom-calendar.scene: Zev leans in a doorway at Friday sundown as a family lights lamps at a long table; nobody has announced anything, the children have simply stopped running and come to the table on their own, and the light in the room has changed

every-song-carries-the-word.scene: Caleb walks a woodland path in low sun with a boy of about eight, the boy carrying a small cased instrument on his back and a worn book under one arm; both objects are being carried together as though it never occurred to anyone to bring only one

what-a-songid-is.scene: Caleb crouches in a vast archive of identical labelled drawers with a girl of about ten, who has pulled one drawer open and found exactly the single card she was looking for; her face is pure vindication

published-before-it-airs.scene: Zev stands on a railway platform at golden hour beside a printed timetable, while all along the platform strangers of every age look up at the same instant as the same thing arrives; two children further down have started the same clapping rhythm at the same moment

how-a-frequency-is-assigned.scene: Jubilee stands at a workshop wall where a hand-drawn dial chart is pinned up, adding one new marker to an empty stretch of it; a small crowd of ordinary people and one very interested child watch her place it

hosted-in-the-language.scene: Santiago sits at a crowded outdoor table mid-story, hands in the air, and the entire table of adults and children is laughing at exactly the right moment — not a beat late, the way a room laughs when nothing had to be explained to it

the-languages-still-missing.scene: Eliana stands before a huge wall map at dusk, most of it pinned with small lights and some of it conspicuously dark; she is reaching up to the dark part, and a teenage girl beside her is writing something down

where-this-band-is-going.scene: Zariah stands at the front of an open-topped sightseeing bus climbing a coast road at golden hour, holding the rail, hair going everywhere, surrounded by tourists of every age; two children at the very front have their arms straight out and are shouting at the view

how-to-use-this-band.scene: Melody sits on a kerb outside a corner shop showing an older man how something works on a cheap phone; a child leaning on her shoulder from behind has clearly already understood it and is trying very hard not to say so

leave-it-on.scene: A wide view through the lit windows of an ordinary house in the evening: in the kitchen Eliana is drying dishes with the mother of the house, in the next room two children are building something on the floor, upstairs a teenager is doing homework — everyone in a different room, all plainly hearing the same thing

for-the-person-who-stopped-going.scene: Nova sits on a park bench beside a man who has clearly not been anywhere near a church in years; there are two coffees, nobody is holding a book, nobody is leaning in, and a dog is trying to get between them

still-being-built-on-purpose.scene: Caleb stands on the deck of a half-finished timber treehouse in golden light with children swarming the ladder below; the structure is obviously unfinished, the children are obviously already using it, and Caleb is hammering the next board in

on-air-today.scene: Imani stands in the middle of a busy market at golden hour, arms wide, mid-laugh, while all around her stallholders and shoppers and running children carry on entirely as normal — everything in the frame is live and happening right now

doubt-is-not-the-opposite-of-faith.scene: Nova stands at the rail of a high suspension bridge in mist with a young man who is gripping the rail hard; she is looking out, relaxed, one hand loose on the cable, and a family with a small child walks past behind them completely unbothered

questions-you-were-told-not-to-ask.scene: Nova sits on the floor of a church hall in a ring of teenagers and two adults, a girl of about fourteen mid-question with her hand still up; every adult in the circle is listening rather than glancing at each other

come-back-without-explaining.scene: Nova stands in the open doorway of a lit house at dusk as a woman with a bag comes up the path after a long absence; nobody is asking anything, a child has already run out past Nova to reach her first

why-midnight-praise-exists.scene: Nova sits alone on a fire escape above a sleeping city at three in the morning, city lights below, one warm window across the street where somebody else is also awake; she is looking at that window rather than at the skyline

hymns-were-written-in-trouble.scene: Nova stands in the doorway of a storm-battered cottage at dawn, the roof visibly patched and the garden wrecked, singing with the elderly couple who live there while their grandchildren drag broken branches into a pile behind them

wisdom-when-advice-runs-out.scene: Nova sits at a hospital corridor window with a man whose advice has plainly run out; neither is speaking, a child asleep across two chairs opposite, the light coming up warm along the corridor floor

nothing-here-closes-the-deal.scene: Nova stands behind a small trestle table at a village fair with nothing on it to sign and nothing to buy, talking to a couple who are free to walk away and are visibly relaxed about it; their child is under the table playing

what-plays-on-the-flagship.scene: Jubilee stands in a crowded lift with eight strangers of wildly different ages and dress — a teenager, a nurse, a man in overalls, a grandmother, a toddler in a pushchair — all of them plainly listening to the same thing and none of them minding

four-generations-one-radio.scene: Jubilee sits at a Sunday table with four visible generations, from a great-grandmother to a baby on a knee, all mid-meal and mid-argument-that-is-really-affection; a single old radio sits on the sideboard and nobody is reaching to change it

decisions-before-you-know.scene: Jubilee walks with a young woman at a fork in a hill path in golden light; the woman has already taken three steps onto one branch without breaking her sentence and has not noticed she chose, while a child ahead runs on regardless

celebrating-without-borrowing.scene: Jubilee dances in a warm garden strung with lights at a family celebration; the joy is enormous and the room is not loud — people are close, faces lit, children spinning, and nothing about it is imported

when-faith-feels-hard-is-not-beginner.scene: Jubilee sits on a workshop step beside a man in his sixties with forty years of wear on his hands, both quiet; he is the experienced one and he is the one having the hard year, and his granddaughter is playing at his feet unaware

never-twice-in-a-day.scene: Jubilee walks a long market street at golden hour where every stall is different from the last; a child ahead of her is running from stall to stall finding something new at each, and nothing in the whole street repeats

jazz-when-nobody-is-performing.scene: Jubilee plays in a back room with three other musicians arranged in a tight circle facing each other rather than outward; there is no audience except one small boy in the doorway, and every player is watching another player's hands

family-faith-is-mostly-logistics.scene: Melody stands in a chaotic hallway at eight in the morning holding one shoe and a lunchbox while three children go in three directions and the dog takes the fourth; she is entirely calm and something is plainly playing through the whole scene

a-sanctuary-that-is-a-kitchen.scene: Melody stands at a kitchen sink in warm evening light while a teenage girl at the table behind her finally starts talking about the thing she came in to say; the room is small, ordinary and completely safe

twenty-minutes-in-the-car.scene: Melody drives at golden hour with a teenage son in the passenger seat, both looking forward at the road rather than at each other, and he is mid-sentence about something that matters; the windscreen light is doing all the work

children-do-not-need-a-simplified-god.scene: Melody kneels to the eye level of a girl of about six who has just asked an enormous question; Melody's face is taking it completely seriously, and the child can obviously tell

beyond-the-trauma-is-not-over-it.scene: Melody walks a beach at low tide with a woman whose footprints are steady beside her own; further up the sand a child is filling in a hole, and the tideline behind them is visibly still there

what-grows-back-and-what-does-not.scene: Melody kneels with two children in a garden where new green is coming up hard around the blackened stump of an old tree that has plainly not returned; the children are entirely focused on the new growth

who-teaches-your-children-the-words.scene: Melody stands in a doorway watching a father sitting on the end of a bed saying words with his small daughter; Melody is not going in, and the picture belongs to the two on the bed

riddim-was-church-first.scene: Zariah plays hand percussion in a packed sanctuary with a drummer, an old woman clapping on the offbeat, and children dancing in the aisle; the rhythm is obviously native to the room rather than borrowed into it

worship-in-a-country-not-yours.scene: Zariah sings in a small back-room congregation on a grey street where hers is the only voice carrying an accent nobody else has; the people around her are warm, and there is a particular loneliness on her face anyway

french-is-not-a-translation.scene: Zariah leans on a balcony rail above a warm evening street where the whole life of the block is different from anywhere else — different pace, different food, different music drifting up; children are playing a game with rules that belong only here

the-commute-belongs-to-you.scene: Zariah stands in a nearly empty train carriage at golden hour with her forehead near the glass, entirely unreachable and entirely at peace; one other passenger further down is asleep and a child is drawing on a foggy window

holidays-hold-the-old-country.scene: Zariah stands in a kitchen full of feast-day cooking where the grandmother is the only one still using every old word; the children are helping with their hands, and the food is doing what the language no longer can

a-rhythm-your-grandmother-knows.scene: Zariah claps a pattern with an elderly woman on a porch while a boy of about seven picks it up on the third try; three generations are doing the same thing and only the youngest is having to learn it

praying-in-the-language-you-dream-in.scene: Zariah sits on the edge of a bed at night having stopped mid-prayer to start again in her first language; the shift is visible on her face, and a sleeping child is curled at the far end of the bed

courage-is-mostly-boring.scene: Caleb is up before dawn in the rain doing the same unremarkable job for what is obviously the hundredth time, with nobody watching except a child in a lit upstairs window who has got up to see him go

iron-requires-two-pieces-of-iron.scene: Caleb spots a friend on the other end of a heavy lift in a plain garage gym; both men are straining, the whole point of the picture is that there are two of them, and a boy sits on a stack of plates watching his father

marriage-matters-is-not-a-conference.scene: Caleb and his wife wash up together on an entirely ordinary Tuesday evening in a small kitchen, elbows touching, mid-conversation about nothing; children's noise is coming from the next room

after-the-storm-nobody-films.scene: Caleb hauls a ruined carpet out of a flood-damaged house months after the rescue, alongside the family who live there and their two children carrying one box between them; there is no crowd and no camera

acapella-when-production-stops.scene: Caleb sings in a bare stairwell with four other people and no instruments at all; the sound is obviously carrying, and a cleaner has stopped on the landing above with her hand on the rail

the-last-ten-minutes-of-the-day.scene: Caleb sits on the floor with his back against a child's bed in the last warm lamplight of the evening, a small hand hanging off the edge of the mattress near his shoulder; the day is ending well on purpose

a-station-not-a-podcast.scene: Caleb runs a familiar route at golden hour past the same corner he passes every day, nodding at the same shopkeeper and the same two children on the same wall; the whole picture is habit rather than event

the-feasts-are-a-calendar.scene: Zev turns the page of a big wall calendar in a family kitchen while children crowd around to see what the next month holds; the calendar is plainly the one running the household

when-the-law-is-set-to-music.scene: Zev walks a market street with a group of children who are chanting a long list to a tune as they go, keeping perfect time with their steps and obviously not finding it a chore

shema-means-hear-then-do.scene: Zev listens to an instruction with his whole body already turning to go and do it; a boy beside him has copied the turn a half second later, and neither has said anything

the-subject-every-station-avoids.scene: Zev sits at a kitchen table with a couple and an open household ledger between them in warm lamplight; nobody is embarrassed, the conversation is plainly happening, and a child is doing homework at the same table

washing-feet-before-anyone-watches.scene: Zev kneels in a back corridor washing the feet of an elderly man before an event begins, with the room beyond still empty and the chairs still stacked; one child who has wandered in is watching from the doorway

identity-is-not-a-personality-type.scene: Zev stands in a hall where a wall of neat category labels has been pinned up and he is standing beside it rather than under any of it; a girl of about twelve has stepped out of the queue to stand beside him

why-heavens-dawn-airs-before-sunrise.scene: Zev walks a hill path in the blue dark before dawn with the first warm line just breaking on the horizon; a sleepy child rides on his shoulders wrapped in a blanket, and the day has clearly already begun

fire-is-not-volume.scene: Imani stands in a congregation at the exact moment it goes quiet, everyone's hands still raised, faces blazing, nobody making a sound; a small girl beside her has her eyes screwed shut in total concentration

ten-days-before-one-day.scene: Imani sits on the floor of an upper room with a dozen ordinary people on day eight of waiting — bedrolls, cold tea, tired faces, somebody's children asleep against the wall — and absolutely nothing has happened yet

africa-is-a-broadcaster.scene: Imani stands at a transmitter mast on a bright African hilltop with the arrows of the picture pointing outward: engineers and singers arriving, equipment being unloaded, children running up the track to see, everything flowing out from here rather than in

what-yoruba-praise-does.scene: Imani leads a call and response in a warm courtyard where the melody visibly changes the meaning of each phrase; the drummers are grinning, and children answer the call a beat ahead of the adults

amharic-worship-is-ancient.scene: Imani stands in a rock-hewn church of enormous age, candlelight on stone, singing with a small congregation of every age; the building is older than almost anything and the music has plainly never left it

praying-in-swahili-at-three.scene: Imani kneels alone in a small lit prayer room at three in the morning while the rest of the building sleeps; through the window one other lit window is visible across the courtyard

chill-is-still-pentecostal.scene: Imani sits absolutely still on a quiet verandah at golden hour with her eyes closed and her hands open on her knees; a child lies on the boards beside her equally still, and the quiet is plainly full rather than empty

la-familia-is-a-doctrine.scene: Santiago stands in the middle of a huge multi-generational family gathering spilling out of a house into the street, babies passed hand to hand, aunts arguing happily, children everywhere; nobody in the picture is a guest

a-latin-station-sung-in-english.scene: Santiago stands on a doorstep between two rooms — one where the older generation is speaking Spanish and one where the teenagers are speaking English — belonging visibly and completely to both, with a child running between them

portuguese-is-not-spanish.scene: Santiago listens closely as two friends demonstrate the difference between two languages to a sceptical teenager, all three talking at once and laughing; the teenager has just heard it and his face has changed

two-generations-one-kitchen.scene: Santiago sits at a kitchen table translating gently between a grandmother and her grandson who each want to say something kind and cannot quite reach the other; both are leaning in

praying-out-loud-as-a-habit.scene: Santiago prays out loud before a meal in a crowded room where everyone including the children joins in without any self-consciousness at all; a visitor at the end of the table looks startled and moved

focus-is-a-discipline.scene: Santiago works at a cluttered desk in complete concentration while ordinary chaos happens around him — a child doing homework, someone on the phone, a delivery at the door — and his attention holds

wellness-without-the-religion.scene: Santiago sits down to a plain good meal with his family after a long walk, boots by the door, everybody hungry and unhurried; there is nothing performative anywhere in the room

arrived-in-the-wrong-hands.scene: Tahoma stands at a weathered mission church on open land at golden hour, one hand flat on the old timber; his face holds two true things at once, and his granddaughter beside him is simply looking up at the building

sobriety-is-a-daily-frequency.scene: Tahoma makes coffee at six in the morning in a plain kitchen, marking one more ordinary day on a wall calendar full of identical marks; his small son is at the table waiting for breakfast

men-with-nowhere-to-be-honest.scene: Tahoma sits in a circle of five men on folding chairs in a bare hall where one of them is finally saying the true answer; nobody is looking away and nobody is fixing it

anxious-no-more-is-a-command.scene: Tahoma sits on a porch step with a young man who is visibly anxious, not instructing him, just sitting; a child plays in the yard and the light is warm on both of them

be-still-is-the-hardest-instruction.scene: Tahoma stands motionless in a rushing river up to his knees in a wetsuit while the water tears past him; everything in the frame is moving except him, and a child watches from the bank

the-rhythm-that-outlasted-the-hymnbook.scene: Tahoma drums at an open-air gathering where the old rhythm is plainly still running the room long after anyone was supervising it; dancers of every age circle, and the children know every step

stories-keep-what-is-not-written.scene: Tahoma tells a story by firelight to a ring of children and adults, hands shaping the air, every face turned to him; there is not a single written thing anywhere in the picture

the-church-already-there.scene: Amir stands inside a very old church on the Indian coast where the congregation is plainly ancient and entirely local; children run between the pillars as though they have always been allowed to

ancient-paths-people-who-looked-like-me.scene: Amir walks a genuinely old stone road through hills at golden hour with a boy of about ten beside him; the road is worn by centuries of feet that looked like theirs

arabic-was-a-language-of-worship.scene: Amir sings in a small ancient chapel where the words carved into the old stone and the words in his mouth are the same language; an elderly woman and two children sing with him

the-bengali-gap-was-indefensible.scene: Amir stands in an immense crowd of ordinary people at a river ghat at golden hour — thousands of faces, families, children everywhere — the sheer number being the entire argument

hindi-worship-is-not-western-worship.scene: Amir sits cross-legged with musicians playing a long circling repetition that is plainly going somewhere rather than filling time; listeners of every age sit close, and a child has fallen asleep against a drum

praying-in-a-language-your-government.scene: Amir sits with a small group in a shuttered room at night, one low lamp, everyone close together and speaking very quietly; a child sleeps against his mother and one man watches the window

what-the-five-fold-actually-is.scene: Amir works alongside four other people building something together on a site, each plainly doing a different job and none of them above the others; a child hands nails up to whoever needs them

repentance-is-a-turn.scene: Elias is caught mid-turn on a hill track, body already committed to the opposite direction, the wrong way still visible behind him; a girl further down the path has already turned and is waiting

country-never-stopped-being-honest.scene: Elias plays guitar on a porch singing something plainly about his own failures to a small gathering of neighbours who are nodding rather than wincing; children sit on the steps below

two-shortest-prayers.scene: Elias shakes hands on an agreement with an older man in a farmyard, both grips firm and both faces serious; a boy watches the handshake closely as though learning what one costs

raising-arrows-no-applause.scene: Elias teaches a boy of about twelve to draw a bow at golden hour on open ground, already looking downrange at where the arrow will go rather than at the boy; nobody else is watching

what-is-given-daily.scene: Elias hands out warm bread from a basket at dawn to a queue of ordinary people who will be back tomorrow; children take theirs with both hands and there is nothing left over to store

churches-that-sang-under-surveillance.scene: Elias sings in a plain room where the singing is deliberately soft and every adult knows exactly why; the children sing at full volume because nobody has told them, and no one stops them

purpose-found-is-usually-assigned.scene: Elias looks up from ordinary work as somebody arrives to tell him what is needed of him; the summons is plainly coming from outside, and a child has run ahead of the messenger to reach him first

strong-and-sober-are-different.scene: Eliana walks uphill with a woman well past the first hard part of stopping, both of them working, both of them steady; a child runs ahead and back again, and the hill is not finished

grief-walked-not-solved.scene: Eliana walks a long empty shoreline at golden hour beside a man carrying something that is not going to be fixed; she is matching his pace exactly and offering nothing else

stillwater-is-not-background-music.scene: Eliana sits beside genuinely still water at dawn with a woman whose whole posture has changed since she sat down; the quiet is plainly doing work rather than filling a gap

friendship-is-a-means-of-grace.scene: Eliana sits on a kitchen floor with her oldest friend, backs against the cupboards, mugs on the tiles, both laughing at something nobody else would find funny; a child steps over their legs unnoticed

japans-tiny-church-old-martyrs.scene: Eliana stands with a very small congregation of about nine people in a modest Japanese room, an ancient memorial stone visible through the window; the group is tiny and the history behind it is enormous

tagalog-travels-with-those-who-leave.scene: Eliana video-calls home from a bright hospital break room at an odd hour, in scrubs, with a birthday plainly happening on the screen and a child on the other end holding up a cake
